title: What OS to put on it
summary: Debian or Ubuntu Server if the box is dedicated. Leave Windows if you still use the laptop as a laptop.

start.body:
An OS (operating system) is what the computer boots into — the software that runs before any apps.

You pick one, install it, and that is what this computer is from then on.

You don't need a new computer to pick an OS. You do need to know how you'll use the box.

gloss.body:
Plain words:

• Install = copy the OS onto the computer's disk so it starts every time
• ISO = the installer file you download (like a disc image)
• Server vs Desktop = text login vs a mouse-and-windows screen

Most home-lab guides assume Debian or Ubuntu. That's why we steer there.

branch.body: How will you use this computer?

choices.label: I already have disks to fill

daily.body:
Leave the OS it has — Windows or macOS.

Don't wipe a machine you still write papers on. You can learn Linux later on a different, spare box.

daily-next.body:
What you can still do this week: read along, mark stack interests, and wait for a spare PC.

When you get one, come back to "Old PC I can dedicate."

dedicated.body:
Install Debian or Ubuntu Server on a dedicated box.

Both are free, boring, and everywhere online. Ubuntu Desktop is fine if you want a screen and a mouse while you learn.

dedicated-pick.body: Pick the flavor that matches your comfort:

ubuntu.body:
Ubuntu Server is the friendly default.

You'll download an ISO from ubuntu.com (look for Server, not Desktop). The next guided project walks the weekend install.

What you'll see later: a black text screen asking for a username — that's normal for Server.

debian.body:
Debian if you want fewer surprise changes between releases.

Slightly less hand-holding than Ubuntu, same idea: a free Linux you leave on. Download the netinst or live ISO from debian.org.

desktop.body:
Ubuntu Desktop is the same family as Server, with icons and a mouse.

Fine while you learn. You can still install server tools later. Download Desktop from ubuntu.com.

download-hint.body:
When you download:

• Prefer the official site (ubuntu.com / debian.org) — not a random mirror blog
• You'll get a big .iso file (a few GB)
• Next weekend: write that file to a USB stick and boot from it

You don't need to burn a real disc.

proxmox.body:
Proxmox lets several "pretend computers" (VMs) share one box.

Not day one unless you already know you want that. Still $0 — but the learning curve is steeper. Most beginners start with plain Ubuntu/Debian first.

proxmox-path.body:
If you're sure: download Proxmox VE from proxmox.com and treat the next weekend like any other OS install.

If you're unsure: pick Ubuntu Server instead — you can add Proxmox later on another disk or box.

choices.label: I'll stick with Ubuntu/Debian for now

nas.body:
TrueNAS, Unraid, and OpenMediaVault are file-box operating systems — great when you have disks to fill.

Later, not this weekend, unless storage is already the whole goal.

nas-path.body:
For a first lab that runs apps and learning commands: Ubuntu/Debian is simpler.

Come back to a NAS OS when you have two+ disks and a clear "I need a file box" job.

stuck-os.body:
If you're stuck choosing:

Default = Ubuntu Server on a spare PC.

That one choice matches the most beginner guides. You can always reinstall later — disks are erasable.

wrap.body:
You've picked a direction for the OS.

Next guided project: your first weekend — USB installer, boot menu, name the machine, reach it from the couch.

end.body: OS choice locked in for now. No shopping required — just a download when you're ready to install.

iso-what.body:
You'll download an .iso — think of it as a complete installer packed into one file.

Later you copy that file onto a USB stick so the computer can boot the installer instead of the old OS.

lts.body:
If Ubuntu offers "LTS" — Long Term Support — pick that.

It means fewer forced jumps and longer security updates. Boring is good.

vm-gloss.body:
VM = virtual machine = a pretend computer inside a real one.

Useful later. On day one, one real OS on bare metal (the actual PC) is simpler.

end-remind.body:
Whatever you picked: write down the name (Ubuntu Server, Debian, Desktop, or other) so the weekend install matches.

Mismatch = wrong ISO on the stick.
